Examples and source quotations are not automatically requirements or certified answers.

## Apply the filing and update protocol

| Event | Record action within authority |
| --- | --- |
| A new capability or consequential rule enters discussion | Assign a recognizable topic and record its question, proposals, evidence and open choices in the topic discussion. Register the record in the catalogue and expose consequential open choices or retained proposals in the work register. |
| An independently identifiable capability or cross-module mechanism is adopted | Reuse its topic design or create a dedicated design document if none fits. Record material choices in the topic decision record and synthesize applicable rules, responsibilities and acceptance before dependent implementation. Register unfinished implementation or verification with its actual disposition. |
| A rule in an existing capability changes | Apply [preservation triggers](#preserve-versions-at-defined-events) before replacing a material adopted rule, then update its owner and [version basis](#bind-design-versions-to-their-basis). Check affected dependencies and replace redundant current restatements with links. Ordinary patches reuse the topic. |
| Research or a verification round completes | Record the method, version, result and limits in its research or verification owner and link from the topic. Update affected work-item dispositions and remaining scope; a check alone does not need a new design or close a whole item. |
| A material finding appears, including an unfixed or unverified one | Record evidence and impact with its detailed owner and add or reconcile the work-register entry even when no remedy is selected; use [discovery guidance](records-and-handoff.md#track-discoveries-without-expanding-the-current-work). |
| A choice is rejected, deferred or superseded | Preserve consequential reasons and evidence, update the register disposition and links, and identify any effective replacement. It does not become pending work merely by remaining recorded. |
| A document is added, moved, split or consolidated | Assign explicit responsibilities, update the catalogue and affected references/tooling, and perform scoped [usability checks](#verify-document-usability). Move detailed ownership rather than creating another maintained copy; preserve necessary provenance and references. |
| An authorized increment closes or hands off | Reconcile affected work items and current readiness, reassess phase readiness and next selection, and finish records with the checks in the same batch. Report actual names, paths and sections, plus unsaved entries or unverified limits; no per-file approval or separate chat is required. |

For example, a streaming capability can have `docs/design/STREAMING_RECEIVE.md` for adopted behavior and `docs/research/YYYYMMDD_HHMM_STREAMING_SIGNALS.md` for one route investigation. Its central topic entry links both and relevant decisions, discussions, findings and verification. The design's revision basis identifies the particular supporting entries, not just their topic or date. A signal investigation alone is not the complete feature design, and a later check does not overwrite the original observations. These paths illustrate the protocol, not permission to move files during a discussion-only task.

## Current guidance and historical versions

Use [the declared classification](#choose-document-responsibilities) to distinguish effective requirements/design, current readiness, observed evidence and historical snapshots. If the user explicitly selects an equivalent arrangement, preserve those distinct responsibilities and the central development entrance.

Describe current design and status directly in active owners. Git preserves ordinary edits; readable history retains the consequential rationale and progression needed to understand a specific version. Decision age alone does not establish obsolescence: record whether it remains effective, is partly or wholly superseded, or is withdrawn, with replacement links and reasons. A historical snapshot preserves a view, not a new competing policy owner. Distinguish facts, hypotheses and later clarifications without inventing chronology or duplicating whole experiment logs.

Consult historical records when relevant, not by default. They can retain valid evidence and reasons for still-applicable decisions; past task permissions, recommendations, commands and unfinished plans are not current execution authority or an automatic backlog. Current human instructions control the authorized task and maintained owners state effective constraints. Check authority, applicability and evidence when records conflict instead of following the newest-looking note or an archived command.

Keep one discoverable current handoff rather than competing instruction copies. A user's selected document structure may be appropriate; neither a separate session-prompt file nor a universal ban on one is required. Apply the scoped preservation triggers below, without requiring a full chat import or a history entry for every session.

## Preserve versions at defined events

Use observable work events within document-write authority rather than relying on an impression that a file is old or long:

| Trigger | Required check and action |
| --- | --- |
| Before replacing a substantive rule in an adopted design | Confirm that the preceding design revision and its basis are directly retrievable. If no suitable preserved version exists, save it before replacement and retain its links. Substantive changes affect applicability, external behavior, data preservation/recovery, permissions, component responsibilities or acceptance guarantees. |
| Before rewriting, moving or consolidating shared rules or discussion/decision content referenced by a design | Check affected design revisions' references. Preserve the applicable rule versions or original source entries with their context and provenance. Keep version-specific links valid; retain a snapshot if the needed content would otherwise be lost or replaced. |
| When consolidating a new adopted revision or preparing its handoff | Check its revision identity, applicable shared rules and decisions/discussions, earlier-version link and adoption versus implementation/verification status under [version basis](#bind-design-versions-to-their-basis). |
| Only spelling, formatting or meaning-preserving clarification changes | Update the active file; ordinary Git history usually suffices. Do not create a substantive revision or snapshot merely for the edit. |

A completed question or decision stage followed by a distinct stage, accumulated history obstructing comprehension, or a need for an exact review/handoff/comparison copy can also justify archiving a coherent discussion stage. Retain its complete material reasoning, objections, counterexamples, evidence and changes of position. Leave a short evolution summary, covered period and direct archive link in the stable active topic file. A new chat, message, fixed length or passage of time alone does not require splitting. Snapshotting an open discussion does not close it; keep its open questions visible in the active owner.

Reuse suitable preserved rule versions and source entries instead of copying every shared document, discussion and decision for each design version. Preserve the dependencies needed to interpret the affected revision; this does not require a whole-project snapshot. Use [historical paths and timestamp meanings](#name-active-and-dated-records); older rules or source entries may remain in active owners when their original content and stable section identity are preserved. Record the snapshot's original owner, capture time, covered scope and any earlier revision identity. Ensure relative links resolve from its saved location and still identify the intended historical basis; disclose locator adjustments rather than claiming an adjusted copy is byte-identical evidence.

Do not append later progress to a captured historical record or silently rewrite what was understood then. Record later corrections in the current owner or a linked correction record, retaining the original claim and evidence. Keep archive locations stable and reconcile any necessary later relocation without silently changing provenance. Recording, preservation and navigation updates belong to the same authorized batch, with no extra approval stage; missing write authority leaves the pending content and intended paths in the response.

## Bind design versions to their basis

Near the top of each adopted topic design, provide a compact **Basis for this revision** section. Use existing identifiers where adequate; a timestamp-form identity such as `20261031_1530` can identify the design revision within its topic. Assign or advance it when the adopted design's meaning changes; cosmetic edits retain it. Distinguish the design identity from implementation versions, verification results and source event times. State its meaning/timezone, retain it in snapshots, and apply the naming section's collision and unknown-time rules without inventing historical identities.

| Item | What the reader must be able to obtain |
| --- | --- |
| Revision and adoption status | Identify the adopted design or target. Link implementation/verification to the applicable versions and evidence; label links showing today's readiness so they do not silently certify an older design. Adoption does not prove completion. |
| Applicable shared rules | Direct links to the preserved versions or stable entries of shared requirements, contracts/APIs, architecture and acceptance rules needed to interpret this revision. Identify the applicable sections and scope. Clearly labeled current-owner links may be added but do not replace the historical basis. |
| Applicable decisions | Direct file/resource and stable section/ID links to all consequential choices needed by this version, including still-effective earlier decisions carried forward. |
| Supporting discussions | Direct links to the relevant questions, important objections, evidence and alternative comparisons, with attribution and adoption scope clear. |
| Changes and preceding version | Explain material changes and retained rules, why they changed, and link the preceding preserved design when one exists. Mark absent or unavailable history honestly. |
| Supporting research or verification | Link applicable evidence and its version/limits when needed to interpret the design; a successful check does not decide a policy. |

A revision may rely on several shared rules, discussions and decisions, and one preserved rule or decision may support many revisions. Bind them explicitly rather than matching timestamps, linking only to a long file's start, or assuming the newest decision replaces all earlier ones. Group related rules where appropriate; no line-by-line source matrix or duplicate evidence ledger is required.

Keep a short design-version list in the active topic design: revision identity, material change and saved-version link. The central catalogue points to this list instead of maintaining another version ledger. Each historical design keeps its own version-specific basis so the reader can follow it directly to the corresponding original entries or snapshots. Snapshot capture time and design revision time may differ; readers must not have to construct a `history/` path or infer correspondence from filenames.

Do not bind a historical design only to mutable current rules, a current-discussion summary or a rewritten decision conclusion. Reuse preserved stable entries where sufficient; before their meaning or location changes, apply the preservation trigger above and ensure historical references still reach the intended content. Verify both current and affected older routes under [document usability](#verify-document-usability). Report unavailable original sources or incomplete mappings rather than fabricating attribution, acceptance or authority.

# Git workflow

Use this when repository work needs a checkpoint, branch or worktree decision, synchronization, integration, release preparation, or cleanup. Proactively recognize these needs during the task so the user does not have to remember each Git operation. Scale the workflow to useful outcomes and preserve existing work.

## Authority and project policy

Protect user data, honor the requested mode, and report version and verification facts accurately. Follow current human instructions and the project's repository policy. Branch names, commit format, merge strategy, primary branch, remote destinations, PR requirements and release cadence belong to the project; this skill supplies decision principles rather than a universal branching model.

[Ticket mode](batch-documents.md#select-one-ticket-mode-for-the-project) selects the task owner. Local tickets are compatible with repository hosting on GitHub and authorized commit, push, PR and merge operations; using that delivery route does not require adopting Issues. Conversely, selecting Issues does not itself authorize any remote operation.

Authorized implementation can include scoped local branches and commits under that policy. Discussion or review alone does not authorize Git mutations, including creating worktrees, fetching into local refs, committing, tagging or cleanup. Use permitted inspection under the [command-effect boundary](review.md#scope-and-authority) and recommend useful next actions. A task outside version control does not automatically need a new or nested repository.

Publishing or changing remote state, and destructive local changes, require applicable authorization. Standing authorization can specify repository, destination refs, operations and conditions; apply it without repeatedly asking. Access to a remote or credentials is not authorization. Requests such as creating a PR or publishing a release may include necessary supporting actions within their stated scope. Prepare a concrete, reviewable result before seeking any missing final approval; ask only about material unresolved authority or choices. A commit does not itself authorize a push, main-branch merge, release or deployment.

For a batch using GitHub, inherit the [project-wide ticket mode](batch-documents.md#select-one-ticket-mode-for-the-project); do not choose a task system per batch. Reuse or establish the relevant execution agreement in its task/coordination owner: repository and base/integration target; branch/worktree needs; permitted issue updates, pushes and PR creation; required checks and merge scope; and closeout conditions. Record only choices that matter, not a new approval form. Use the environment's branch naming convention (such as `codex/` in Codex) unless the user/project selects another. Do not assume the shared branch is named `main`.

Interpret delivery requests by their actual effects. "Implement locally" supports scoped local checkpoints and integration. "Implement and open a PR" can include the necessary task-branch push and PR creation; it does not imply shared-branch merge. "Draft PR text" remains a local/response artifact, whereas "open a draft PR" creates a remote object. Issue creation/maintenance and merge follow their separately applicable task or standing authority. Do not ask again for operations already covered, or infer a new repository-wide publication policy from one completed task.

## Recognize decision points

| Point in the work | Assess and act within scope |
| --- | --- |
| Start or resume | Confirm repository, working directory, branch/HEAD, existing changes and relevant active worktrees. Establish the intended base and integration target. |
| Scope grows or an alternative emerges | Consider a branch for independently reviewable work or a discardable experiment. Preserve current work before separating it. |
| Another version must be used concurrently | Assess a worktree and its setup/storage cost; first look for a suitable existing checkout. |
| A coherent improvement or validation boundary is reached | Inspect the intended diff, create an appropriate local checkpoint, and assess pending synchronization. |
| Handoff, end of an increment, or substantial refactor ahead | Ensure useful work is recoverable; proactively identify uncommitted or unsynchronized work and any usable baseline worth marking. |
| Verified phase completion | Check checkpoints and pending synchronization/integration; assess a milestone or release and retain stable completion anchors under [Rolling phase plans](records-and-handoff.md#maintain-a-rolling-phase-plan). |
| A useful workflow is verified or an install/distribution is planned | Assess milestone/tag or release readiness, actual artifacts and rollback needs. |
| Branch/worktree work ends | Integrate and verify, retain it for an explicit purpose, or safely remove it. |

These are decision triggers, not mandatory operations at every turn. An ordinary small edit may use the current branch; a new development phase alone does not require another branch or worktree.

## Preserve work and make useful checkpoints

Inspect existing staged, unstaged and untracked changes before selecting what to commit. Include intended code, tests and affected maintained guidance; preserve unrelated changes and their ownership. Review the staged diff rather than staging the entire checkout by habit. If changes share a file, use safe hunk selection or a proportionate snapshot; ask when their ownership or required treatment cannot be established. A dirty checkout is not permission to discard work.

Commit at coherent boundaries that another reader can explain, inspect and recover. Several completed increments should not silently accumulate in one uncommitted diff. Incomplete but useful work may have an explicitly labeled checkpoint. Describe what changed and why, and retain the actual checks and limitations in the appropriate record. Commit frequency follows the work, not a per-file or per-message quota.

For tests and reviews, identify the relevant commit plus any remaining changes, or an exact snapshot when appropriate. Include required untracked files; HEAD alone cannot identify an uncommitted implementation. A commit is a recovery point, not proof of passing tests or accepted output. Apply the [project storage policy](artifacts-and-storage.md#plan-storage-when-the-project-starts), preserving necessary versioned records and shareable evidence separately from private inputs and disposable outputs. A private remote does not make sensitive data suitable for Git. Do not change global configuration or ignore maintained documentation merely to make a commit convenient. [Source and execution identities](artifacts-and-storage.md#distinguish-source-versions-from-execution-evidence) explain why a synchronized source revision does not by itself back up a run or package.

Record the version being described, not an endlessly changing latest `HEAD`: a document in commit B can accurately identify implementation/verification commit A. Do not require a tracked file to contain the SHA of its own containing commit or repeatedly commit status edits just to keep a "fully synchronized" claim current. A planned tag name is not an existing tag; verify the created tag's target before reporting it as established. Follow project policy for versioning maintained state documents; avoiding self-reference does not require making them untracked. These rules prescribe no fixed commit/tag sequence and do not transfer A's verification to changed code in B without checking applicability.

## Choose and close branches and worktrees

A branch separates a line of changes; a worktree supplies another simultaneous checkout. Prefer reusing a suitable existing location. Use a branch when independent review, integration or experimentation benefits; add a worktree when concurrent checkouts or preserving ongoing work justifies it. If the need becomes apparent after edits begin, preserve the current state and choose a safe separation rather than restarting the work.

If the current `HEAD` is the intended base and edits should remain in this checkout, `git switch -c <new-branch>` can retain the index and working-tree changes while creating the branch. It does not save uncommitted work or separate inherited commits. A different base requires deliberate preservation and transfer of the intended changes. If switching refuses, inspect the conflict rather than adding discard flags.

For a WIP commit or stash, verify exactly what is saved and how it will be recovered. Plain stash excludes untracked files; `-u` includes untracked but not ignored files. Preserve useful ignored files separately when needed; do not blindly use `--all`, which can put private inputs or credentials into Git storage. Keep the saved identity discoverable and verify restoration before discarding a temporary recovery copy.

Follow project or management-tool conventions for worktree names and locations. If none exists, choose a consistent parent location and a short, unique purpose-based name; report the actual path. Do not relocate managed worktrees merely to fit an example naming format.

Before adding a worktree, establish its task, owner, base, destination branch and expected end condition. A checkout of a commit does not include another checkout's uncommitted edits: deliberately preserve or transfer needed changes and verify the intended source state. Use the returned working directory consistently. Account for duplicated dependencies, virtual environments, builds and datasets; arrange mutable task data/configuration appropriately without copying secrets into versioned files. Worktrees share repository state and are not security sandboxes.

For concurrent writes, give each worktree its own task branch and coordinate one owner per branch; do not bypass Git's checked-out-branch protection to put concurrent writers on the same branch. Pass the implementer the exact path, source basis, permitted files/interfaces, integration target and expected returned commits/checks. For dependent ticket B, start from the integrated prerequisite A or deliberately transfer A and verify that basis. Independent C can proceed from its suitable basis. Read-only review often needs no extra checkout. [Delegation](delegation.md#coordinate-shared-work) owns dispatch and return coordination.

Avoid creating a worktree for every phase, review or agent by default. More worktrees need a concrete benefit, not a universal numerical cap. Keep purpose and integration status discoverable through existing task attachments or project records; a separate registry is not mandatory. Only reuse a checkout compatible with its current owner and active work.

When finished, inspect whether the intended work is integrated, intentionally retained, or superseded. Check equivalence when squash or cherry-pick was used; branch reachability alone may not explain integration. An abandoned experiment need not be merged, but preserve useful findings and decide what happens to its changes. Before removal, account for uncommitted/untracked files, necessary ignored data and detached or unpushed commits. A clean tracked diff alone does not establish that a directory is disposable.

Close out worktrees you created within authorized scope using the supported lifecycle tools. Confirm the path, lack of active use and recoverable disposition of useful work before deletion. For another task's worktree, an unclear owner or uncertain valuable content, inspect and propose a disposition rather than deleting it. Report retained worktrees with a reason and next action; do not leave their cleanup implicit. Removing a worktree and deleting its branch are separate decisions.

Cleanup includes disposable worktree-local environments, dependencies and build caches after checking for useful data and shared locations or link targets; directory names alone do not establish disposability. With raw Git, prefer `git worktree remove` for a linked checkout. Use `git worktree prune` only for stale administrative records of missing worktrees, inspecting `--dry-run` when useful. It does not remove existing checkouts or dependency caches and is not a mandatory follow-up to normal removal.

## Integrate and recover deliberately

Follow the actual history and project convention when choosing merge, rebase, squash or cherry-pick. Check the target and preserve unrelated work. Resolve conflicts according to intended behavior and requirements; accepting one side wholesale or obtaining a conflict-free merge does not establish correctness. Verify the integrated result proportionately, especially when combining independently tested changes.

For a multi-ticket batch, identify the shared integration target and each contribution's source basis. Before accepting a contribution, inspect changes since that basis and reconcile affected interfaces, generated files and tests. A shared checkout can serve the integration target; a separate branch/worktree is useful only when the project's work requires it. Record which checks cover the resulting combined state, and rerun affected checks when integration changes their assumptions. Coordinate one integrator for overlapping changes under [delegation](delegation.md#coordinate-shared-work).

Before amend/rebase, establish whether history is private or shared, who depends on it, and which tested/reviewed identities must remain traceable. Rewriting shared history, force-pushing, deleting refs or discarding files needs authorization covering the affected work. `--force-with-lease` is a guard against an unexpected remote ref, not permission to rewrite history.

Choose a scoped recovery method that preserves useful later work. Reverting a change, inspecting an older version and resetting a branch have different effects. Do not use broad reset/clean/restore operations to bypass conflicts or make tests pass. Preserve a recoverable state and make the affected scope clear before an authorized destructive operation.

## Synchronize and remind proactively

At the decision points above, determine whether valuable work remains uncommitted, committed only locally, synchronized, or awaiting integration. Inspect the intended remote, target refs and actual outgoing commits, including inherited commits, rather than only the latest commit. Consider relevant large-file objects and publication/CI effects. Check divergence before choosing the next action.

Fetch retrieves remote objects and updates local tracking refs; it does not integrate them into the working branch. Pull fetches and then integrates. Within authorized implementation/synchronization, obtain the needed remote state, inspect divergence and preserve local work before selecting a fast-forward, merge or rebase under project policy. Do not run a blind pull into an active or dirty checkout, assume a clean checkout is current, or treat a cached tracking ref as a fresh remote observation.

When synchronization is appropriate and authorized, perform it and verify the resulting remote refs and relevant objects. If a network result is ambiguous, inspect the remote state before repeating a mutation. Respect repository hooks and branch protection. Do not silently expand a push to other branches, tags, remotes, or history rewriting.

When authorization is missing, actively remind the user with the observed state, destination, useful reason and concrete next step. For example: a completed batch still needs a local checkpoint before push; or a verified set of local commits is ready to synchronize. Use real counts and identities. Cached tracking refs can be stale; refresh or query within scope, and say synchronization is unconfirmed when evidence is insufficient. Report synchronization for the specific commits/refs and time checked; recheck volatile counts when they matter. Never describe local work as remotely backed up without verification.

Avoid nagging about unchanged state each turn. Respect an explicit deferral and reconsider when new work, a meaningful handoff or a changed condition warrants it. Preserve a consequential deferred action in an existing owner only when record updates are authorized. These checks occur during active work and closeout; they do not create a background monitor or scheduled reminder.

## Publish, review and merge the selected result

Use local Git tooling for checkout/history operations and the available GitHub integration for issues, PRs and checks. If a connector lacks a required operation, use an available supported CLI/API within the same authority, or report the specific limit. Reconcile the repository, head and base before writing; a local branch name does not identify the intended remote PR by itself.

Before an authorized push, inspect all outgoing commits and the relevant diff, then verify the destination ref after publication. Create or update the intended PR with [the delivery explanation](implementation.md#explain-delivery-and-prepare-a-pr), spec/issue links and actual checks. Reuse an existing matching PR. Draft PRs remain explicitly draft until ready and within the requested publication scope; a draft cannot merge. Apply [issue closure rules](github-issues.md#connect-prs-and-close-against-evidence) rather than adding closing keywords to every related issue.

For a requested delivery through PR review, inspect current checks and review findings, correct supported scoped defects, push permitted corrections and recheck the affected result. Tie review and check evidence to the actual head; a later fix or conflict resolution can invalidate earlier coverage. A local agent review does not fabricate an independent GitHub approval. Missing required human review or unavailable CI is a concrete remaining condition, not permission to bypass protection or keep making speculative edits.

Merge the published PR only within applicable merge authority, using the project's allowed strategy and required checks/reviews or merge queue. Reconfirm the intended base, current head and applicable acceptance immediately before merging; where supported, guard the merge against a changed head. Combining task commits into a local batch branch is distinct from merging that published batch into the shared branch. Do not enable auto-merge, bypass protections or rewrite shared history as an unrequested workaround.

Verify the actual merge result and resulting target revision. Run required post-merge checks within scope, then close eligible issues and reconcile readiness. If the task ends at PR creation or review, report that achieved boundary and the remaining merge/acceptance work. Close or retain task worktrees under [their lifecycle](#choose-and-close-branches-and-worktrees), accounting for useful unpushed or ignored data; remote branch deletion is a separate authorized operation. Merge does not imply release or deployment.

If a required post-merge check fails, retain or reopen the affected issue and record the actual merged revision and failure. Continue diagnosis and scoped correction under existing batch authority through [the delivery loop](implementation.md#deliver-the-agreed-batch); do not stop merely because the first PR merged or ask again for an already-authorized repair. Any further push/PR/merge still follows its applicable scope, which may cover only a named PR or may cover the whole batch. Isolate any genuinely missing decision or authority after completing permitted work, and preserve valid narrower acceptance separately from the failed batch condition.

## Mark usable versions and prepare releases

Distinguish a development checkpoint, a named usable milestone and a published release. Proactively assess a tag/version record or release when a complete useful workflow has been verified, an important user-facing fix is ready, installation/distribution is intended, or a substantial upcoming change needs a recoverable baseline. Choose the level justified by actual usability; passing unit tests alone does not establish release readiness.

Use project naming/versioning conventions. A milestone may be useful before formal publication. Within authority, prepare or create the appropriate version marker and release materials; otherwise recommend a concrete milestone or release with its evidence and remaining needs. An old release label does not establish that its build contains current source changes.

Tie release source to an explicit commit/tag and the relevant dependency locks, build conditions, actual artifacts and verification. Check that the intended assets correspond to that version and can be retrieved after an authorized publication. Preserve the distinction between preparing a draft, publishing a release, distributing an artifact and installing/deploying it. Keep release notes accurate about improvements, known limits and applicable migration steps; do not quietly move an existing published tag to new code.

For rollback, retain the previous usable code identity and necessary artifact/configuration information. Assess data/schema migrations, saved-file compatibility and external effects when they apply. Restoring code alone may not restore earlier data or reverse a migration. Document and proportionately verify the applicable recovery route and its limits; do not promise rollback based only on a tag or impose a full deployment system on every small project. Reconcile affected phase/current-state claims under [Rolling phase plans](records-and-handoff.md#maintain-a-rolling-phase-plan); rollback alone does not invalidate historical verification of another version.

## Closeout and references

Briefly report the relevant branch/checkpoint, verification, synchronization/integration state, release identity or recommendation, and remaining worktree disposition. Include only meaningful items, with a concrete next action where needed. Keep project records under their existing owners as described in [Documentation and handoff](records-and-handoff.md#keep-records-proportional-and-recoverable). These status distinctions support continuation; they do not require a separate Git diary or a long checklist each turn.

For uncertain command or hosting behavior, consult the applicable official documentation. Useful starting points are [Git worktree](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree), [Git switch](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-switch), [Git stash](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-stash), [Git pull](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-pull), [Git push](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-push), [GitHub PR merging](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/merging-a-pull-request), and [GitHub releases](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/about-releases). They explain mechanisms; current user instructions and project policy determine authorization.

# GitHub Issues and delivery tracking

Use this when GitHub Issues is the selected ticket destination or work register. [Tickets](implementation.md#turn-a-spec-into-tickets) defines work decomposition; this reference maps that work to GitHub. Follow [Git authority](git-workflow.md#authority-and-project-policy) for remote changes. A request to discuss or split work does not by itself select GitHub or publish issues. The skill guides an active agent; issues and dependency links do not themselves launch agents or enforce execution order.

## Choose the ownership map

Use this execution arrangement only when the project has selected `github-issues` under [project ticket mode](batch-documents.md#select-one-ticket-mode-for-the-project). Keep the [fixed batch directory](batch-documents.md#use-fixed-paths-for-every-batch) for every batch; size or temporary service availability cannot select local tickets for an individual batch.

| Owner | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Batch `spec.md` and linked topic designs | Batch criteria and adopted behavior, constraints and rationale in their respective owners. |
| Batch `tickets.md` | Stable ticket IDs and Issue links; no mirrored task content, dependencies or execution state. |
| Batch parent issue, when useful | Batch coordination and child relationships; links to `spec.md` and `verification.md`, without another acceptance verdict. |
| Child or standalone issue | A verifiable contribution, dependencies, responsible role and execution state; links to criteria and observed results. |
| WORK_ITEMS | Cross-topic problems, selections, deferrals and next actions; link execution issues instead of duplicating their changing task lists. |
| PHASE_PLAN and CURRENT_STATE | Phase direction/acceptance and interaction continuation respectively; neither mirrors Issue progress. |
| PR | The proposed change and review/merge activity; links to tickets and verification. |
| Batch `verification.md` | Observed results or exact existing-evidence links, source identity and limits; the single combined acceptance verdict. |

An explicitly selected GitHub tracker can instead own the entire project work register. Document that mapping in the development entry and reconcile existing records within migration authority. Do not silently replace a mandated WORK_ITEMS owner. In the mixed arrangement above, local entries own cross-topic selection/disposition and link execution issues; they do not reproduce issue progress. Apply [one owner per fact](documentation-structure.md#keep-one-owner-per-fact): references contain descriptive links, not manually maintained summaries or copies of another owner's criteria, results or verdict.

Keep substantive technical rules and necessary engineering explanations in versioned project documents so they remain understandable from the repository. Issues link to them and retain operational coordination. Use GitHub-accessible paths and anchors; an unpublished local file is not a usable issue link. For work in progress, identify the branch/PR document and its pending status; use the actual spec/code revision for acceptance evidence. Do not push merely to manufacture a link outside publication scope.

## Create useful issues and relationships

Before creation, inspect the selected repository and relevant existing issues, work IDs and active claims. Reuse or link an existing item rather than generating a duplicate. Give it a stable identifying title and link the exact outcome/problem, spec/finding basis, acceptance criterion and evidence owners. Write task-specific prerequisites, responsibility and execution state in the issue. If a necessary task criterion has no owner yet, define it once in the fitting owner; do not leave a chain of empty references. Preserve existing project IDs alongside issue numbers when correspondence matters. A defect can be recorded before its remedy is selected; an issue's existence does not authorize implementation.

Use a parent with sub-issues for a batch that benefits from independent tracking. A small fix can be one issue with a concise checklist. Do not create an issue per edit, mandatory layer, agent or test. Native sub-issue relationships express containment; native blocked-by/blocking relationships express prerequisites. Keep those meanings distinct and continue independent ready work. If the available integration cannot maintain a native relationship, retain explicit issue links and describe the limitation rather than claiming the relationship was created.

Issue, agent, branch, worktree and PR counts need not match. Several coupled tickets can share one branch/PR; one issue may need several contributions. GitHub assignees identify actual accounts, not transient subagent names. Record agent responsibility and checkout/source details in the existing execution owner under [delegation](delegation.md#coordinate-shared-work); do not assign an arbitrary account to simulate an agent claim.

## Maintain progress during execution

The main agent reads the selected work, reconciles dependencies and ownership, dispatches ready work within delegation authority, and maintains important transitions through [batch delivery](implementation.md#deliver-the-agreed-batch). Keep ready, active, blocked, implemented-awaiting-integration and accepted work distinguishable using existing labels, issue text or an already-selected Project. These are workflow distinctions, not universal built-in issue states; a Project board is optional.

Update the issue's own execution facts at assignment, a material blocker/dependency change, integration, deferral and closure. Link the actual branch/commit/PR and evidence when available; a new evidence entry usually needs a link rather than its result copied into an issue comment. Follow [transition synchronization](records-and-handoff.md#maintain-documents-throughout-the-work). Avoid per-tool-call comments and mirrored acceptance/progress checklists. Preserve other contributors' content and active ownership; refresh a remotely edited issue before replacing its body. After an ambiguous create/update response, inspect the destination before retrying to avoid duplicate issues or comments.

Scoped review defects return to correction and rechecking within the batch. Separate suggestions retain an unselected or deferred disposition with reasons and a revisit condition. Existing remote write authority covers routine in-scope issue maintenance without another approval per update; local automatic documentation alone grants no remote publication authority. If the service or authorization is unavailable, preserve pending updates in the permitted owner, identify the stale remote state, and continue independent authorized work.

## Connect PRs and close against evidence

Reference the issues addressed by a PR and identify which acceptance conditions the actual changes cover. Use an ordinary reference such as `Refs #123` when work is partial or required checks follow merge. GitHub interprets closing keywords such as `Closes #123` in PR descriptions when the PR targets the repository's default branch; merging into a batch integration branch does not provide that automatic closure. Use a closing link only when its merge event corresponds to the issue's completion condition. Manually linked closing relationships can also close issues, so avoid them when post-merge acceptance must remain open.

Follow [PR and merge delivery](git-workflow.md#publish-review-and-merge-the-selected-result) for current source, checks and merge authority. A PR being opened, a worker returning, or a child issue closing does not establish whole-batch acceptance. Close a batch parent only after all selected acceptance conditions have evidence, including required integration or post-merge checks. A PR-only task may finish with acceptance work still open; report that boundary without claiming the entire product outcome is accepted.

When closing within authority, link the acceptance owner containing the result, tested revision, evidence and limits; do not repeat that report in the issue. Distinguish completion from duplicate, rejected or superseded closure and preserve links. If later evidence invalidates acceptance, reopen or create a linked follow-up as appropriate, preserving the earlier result and changed conditions in their owners. Reassess affected independently owned WORK_ITEMS/CURRENT_STATE decisions without mirroring issue state or rewriting historical evidence.
